text: ASCII, defined in 1963, used 7 bits to give 128 numeric slots for characters, so a capital A is 65, a lowercase a is 97, and a space is 32. Those 128 slots only cover English letters, basic punctuation, and a few control codes, so there is no room for accented letters like e-acute, Chinese characters, or emoji.
title: aadhar.sh: UTF-8

text: Unicode gives every character one universal number called a code point, written in the form U+XXXX. For example, A is U+0041, the Chinese character zhong is U+4E2D, and the grinning-face emoji is U+1F600, covering roughly 150,000 characters and growing. A code point is still just a number, so a separate decision about how to store it as bytes is what an encoding actually is.
title: aadhar.sh: UTF-8

text: UTF-32 stores every code point as exactly 4 bytes, which makes indexing trivial because each character is the same fixed width. The cost is wasted space: plain English text becomes 4 times bigger (an A is stored as 00 00 00 41), and it breaks ASCII compatibility, so older tools and files that expect single-byte ASCII choke on it.
title: aadhar.sh: UTF-8

text: UTF-8 is variable-width: 1 byte for ASCII characters, 2 bytes for most Latin and accented letters, 3 bytes for most CJK characters like the Chinese zhong, and 4 bytes for emoji and rare scripts. Because the 1-byte case is identical to ASCII, old English text stays byte-for-byte the same, giving backwards compatibility for free.
title: aadhar.sh: UTF-8

text: UTF-8 is self-synchronizing: every byte announces whether it is a start byte or a continuation byte, so a reader that drops into the middle of a stream can still find where the next character begins. In a single UTF-8 character, the leading byte carries a prefix that says how many bytes the character spans, and each continuation byte starts with the bits 10, so reading the payload bits from each byte in order rebuilds the original code point.
title: aadhar.sh: UTF-8

text: In UTF-8 a CJK character such as the Chinese zhong is 3 bytes but still one code point and usually one visual glyph, so the length of text depends on whether you count bytes, code points, or grapheme clusters. Indexing Chinese characters by byte position is error-prone for exactly this reason, which is why the four-corner method indexes characters by the shape of strokes in each corner rather than by their bytes or pronunciation.
title: aadhar.sh: UTF-8

text: UTF-8 encodes characters using a variable width of 1 to 4 bytes. A single-byte character uses the binary form 0xxxxxxx and matches ASCII exactly; a two-byte character uses 110xxxxx followed by 10xxxxxx; three bytes use 1110xxxx plus two 10xxxxxx continuation bytes; and four bytes use 11110xxx plus three continuation bytes. The leading byte's prefix length tells a reader how many continuation bytes follow, which is what makes the encoding self-synchronizing.
title: UTF-8 (Wikipedia)

text: UTF-8 has been the most common character encoding on the World Wide Web since 2008, and as of early 2026 it is used by roughly 99 percent of surveyed websites. The first 128 Unicode code points map directly to ASCII, so a UTF-8 file that uses only those characters is byte-for-byte identical to an ASCII file.
title: UTF-8 (Wikipedia)

text: A code point is a numeric value assigned to a specific character within a coded character set. In Unicode, code points are written with the U+ prefix followed by a hexadecimal value, such as U+0041 for the letter A, and an encoding then determines how each code point becomes actual bytes: UTF-32 uses a fixed 4 bytes, UTF-16 uses one or two 2-byte units, and UTF-8 uses one to four bytes.
title: Code point (Wikipedia)

text: Unicode is a character encoding standard, maintained by the Unicode Consortium, that aims to support text in all of the world's writing systems. Its codespace runs from U+0000 to U+10FFFF, providing more than 1.1 million possible code points, of which Version 17.0 (September 2025) assigns about 159,801 characters across 172 scripts. Unicode itself only maps characters to numbers; UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 are the transformation formats that turn those numbers into bytes.
title: Unicode (Wikipedia)
